paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of identifying event-related brain responses when recordings contain noise and the response patterns can change during a session. Its approach uses a competitive neural network to discover patterns within the recordings, rather than requiring the data to be divided into stimulus-related groups beforehand.

As learning proceeds, the network weights converge toward the signal patterns embedded in the data. Those learned weights form a bank of matched filters: each filter is suited to detecting a particular pattern. This connects learning and identification directly, because the patterns the network discovers become the templates it uses to recognize responses.

The authors investigate robustness at low signal-to-noise ratios through simulations and compare performance with information-theoretic expectations. They also apply the classifier to recordings from an odd-ball experiment. The reported result is automatic identification of patterns that vary within a session, removing the stated requirement for advance stimulus-based grouping and allowing the recorded signals themselves to determine the categories.
neurips-1997-a-generic-approach-for-iden.tldr: A competitive neural network learns brain-response templates and identifies changing patterns without advance stimulus-based grouping.

paragraphs: Filial imprinting provides a way to study how rapid learning interacts with an animal's built-in preferences. Domestic chicks do not approach learning with entirely neutral interests: the abstract describes a visual preference for heads and necks that develops during their first three days. The paper models how this predisposition can coexist with learning about a particular object.

The authors construct a neural network model designed to remain consistent with existing knowledge about imprinting-related learning. This is a meaningful constraint because the neurological basis of imprinting is described as relatively clear, while the basis of the visual predisposition is largely unknown. The model connects these two processes within one computational account.

The network develops the preference, learns to approach a training object, and reproduces one interaction between predisposition and imprinting. These results show that the two forms of behavior can be represented together. The authors identify reproducing additional interactions and explaining why the system works as future work, so the demonstrated account covers a specific part of their relationship.
neurips-1997-a-neural-network-model-of-n.tldr: A neural network models how chicks develop an early visual preference while learning to approach an imprinted object.

paragraphs: Natural images occupy a structured part of the space of possible images. Their visual organization means that some arrangements occur much more often than others. The paper starts from the idea that capturing this uneven distribution can support several tasks, including recognizing images and removing noise from them.

The authors introduce a statistical image model described as non-parametric and multi-scale. The multi-scale aspect makes structure at different image scales part of the modeling approach. The motivation is to address a tension in earlier statistical methods, which the abstract describes as restricted either in the complexity of their models or in the complexity of the images they could handle.

The proposed model can be used for recognition, denoising, and generating textures. These uses connect understanding observed images with producing new image content through the same statistical framework. The abstract specifically reports synthesis of high-quality textures. Its broader contribution is a model intended to capture useful natural-image structure across several image-processing purposes, rather than serving only one task.
neurips-1997-a-non-parametric-multi-scal.tldr: A non-parametric image model captures structure across scales for recognition, denoising, and texture synthesis.

paragraphs: Predicting a changing system becomes difficult when measurements arrive only occasionally and at irregular intervals. For nonlinear systems with randomness, accounting for the unobserved values can require integrals that have no analytical solution. The paper addresses this obstacle in both prediction and maximum-likelihood learning.

The proposed model combines a nonlinear recurrent neural predictor with a linear model of its errors. This particular combination makes the prediction and adaptation rules tractable. The recurrent component is trained with real-time recurrent learning, while the error component uses expectation-maximization implemented through forward-backward Kalman filtering equations. The two components therefore handle different parts of the modeling problem.

The authors apply the approach to a diabetic patient's glucose and insulin metabolism, with blood glucose measured only a few times daily at irregular times. They report considerable improvement over recurrent networks trained through teacher forcing or free-running prediction, as well as several linear models. The result supports combining nonlinear prediction with structured error modeling when observations are sparse and unevenly spaced.
neurips-1997-a-solution-for-missing-data.tldr: Combining a recurrent predictor with a linear error model makes learning from irregularly missing measurements tractable.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making problems in which an agent cannot directly observe the full state of its environment. A policy must guide actions despite that incomplete information. The authors develop a policy iteration algorithm that repeatedly evaluates a policy and then improves it, with an emphasis on simplifying these operations.

The key choice is to represent a policy as a finite-state controller. This gives the policy a concrete form that makes evaluation straightforward. The central contribution then connects policy improvement to the same representation: the dynamic-programming update can be understood as transforming the existing controller into a better controller. Evaluation and improvement thus operate within one consistent description of the policy.

The resulting algorithm is described as simpler and more efficient than the earlier policy iteration approach discussed in the abstract. It also consistently outperforms value iteration on infinite-horizon problems. The finding emphasizes that choosing a useful policy representation can improve the practical process of solving ongoing decision problems under partial observability.
neurips-1997-an-improved-policy-iteratio.tldr: Representing policies as finite-state controllers yields a simpler, more efficient policy iteration algorithm for partially observable decisions.

paragraphs: Densely connected Bayesian networks make exact inference computationally difficult. One practical alternative is mean-field approximation, which replaces a complicated distribution with a simpler one and supports a bound on the log likelihood. The paper focuses on the representational restriction imposed by using a single factorized approximation.

The authors propose mixing several mean-field distributions. Each component retains a simple form, while their combination provides a richer approximation than any one component alone. This matters when uncertainty cannot be adequately represented by the unimodal form assumed in the basic approach. The paper also derives an efficient algorithm for updating the mixture parameters, making the richer representation usable for learning.

The method is applied to sigmoid belief networks. The reported results improve systematically over simple mean-field theory as more mixture components are included. This connects the added expressive capacity to observed benefits: increasing the number of components gives the approximation more flexibility while preserving an efficient parameter-update procedure.
neurips-1997-approximating-posterior-dis.tldr: Mixtures of mean-field distributions provide richer posterior approximations that improve as additional components are introduced.

paragraphs: Combining sensory channels can fail when the environment changes in ways their recognition modules do not expect. The abstract describes a particularly damaging behavior: a module operating outside its assumptions can gain influence over the combined result. The paper calls this catastrophic fusion and seeks a principled way to control it.

The proposed Bayesian approach gives each sensory channel simple context models based on white noise. It estimates the perceptual interpretation and the context together. When a channel deviates from its expected conditions, the model interprets that deviation through the strength of noise contamination. This allows the channel's influence to adjust automatically as part of inference.

The authors test the method on audiovisual speech recognition with a fixed vocabulary and report very good results. The central contribution is to make channel reliability part of the recognition model itself. Audio and visual evidence are combined while simultaneously assessing the conditions under which each was obtained, addressing the source of the fusion failure.
neurips-1997-bayesian-robustification-fo.tldr: Jointly estimating sensory interpretations and noise conditions helps prevent unreliable channels from dominating audiovisual recognition.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis identifies major directions of variation in data. When observations have many dimensions and there are many of them, efficiently extracting just a few of those directions becomes valuable. The paper presents an expectation-maximization algorithm for obtaining a small set of eigenvectors and eigenvalues from such datasets.

The algorithm is described as efficient in both memory use and computation, and it naturally accommodates missing information. The paper also introduces sensible principal component analysis, or SPCA. This variant defines a proper probability density over the data space, giving the representation an explicit statistical interpretation. SPCA is trained using an expectation-maximization algorithm as well.

Results on synthetic and real data show that the algorithms recover the leading covariance eigenvectors correctly and efficiently in a few iterations. The reported applications reach hundreds of thousands of observations with thousands of dimensions. Together, these contributions connect scalable extraction of principal directions with handling incomplete observations and constructing a density model.
neurips-1997-em-algorithms-for-pca-and-s.tldr: EM algorithms efficiently recover principal components, accommodate missing data, and support a density-model variant called SPCA.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a hierarchical generative model that extends factor analysis to nonlinear relationships and can be implemented as a neural network. Its goal is to infer underlying structure from perceptual input while keeping the inference consistent with the model's probabilities.

Inference uses connections running upward, downward, and laterally through the network. These connections can be learned with simple rules that depend only on information available locally. The authors also explain how lateral connections can be incorporated into the generative model itself. This links the network's communication structure to the statistical account of how observations are produced.

On simplified random-dot stereograms, the model learns a sparse, distributed representation of depth across its hierarchy. Local disparity detectors in its first hidden layer become organized into a topographic map. With natural-scene image patches, it also develops topographically arranged local feature detectors. The results connect probabilistic perceptual learning with the emergence of spatial organization among the network's learned detectors.
neurips-1997-hierarchical-non-linear-fac.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic neural model learns depth representations and topographic feature maps using locally available information.

paragraphs: The paper models spatial behavior in rats using two watermaze tasks. One is the standard task; the other introduces novel platform locations and a more demanding learning requirement. In the latter, rats show learning from a single trial after several days of training. The model therefore addresses rapid learning that emerges after prior experience.

Its central components are hippocampal place cells, used both to support reinforcement learning and to construct and use allocentric coordinates. Allocentric coordinates describe location relative to the surrounding environment. The approach integrates these uses of spatial information, bringing together learning through reinforcement and an environment-based representation of position within the same model.

The title identifies temporal-difference learning as the reinforcement-learning approach. The abstract's main contribution is the integrated account of place-cell-supported learning and coordinates across the two tasks. The novel-platform task makes the relationship especially relevant: the behavior to be modeled includes adapting to a new location after earlier training, alongside performance in the standard watermaze setting.
neurips-1997-hippocampal-model-of-rat-sp.tldr: A rat navigation model integrates place-cell-supported reinforcement learning with environment-based spatial coordinates.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how relationships between words and text passages can support the learning of human-like knowledge. It uses singular value decomposition to learn from large collections of word occurrences. The method is interpreted as unsupervised training of a network that associates words and passages through a single hidden layer with linear connections.

The learned representation places words and passages in semantic spaces with 100 to 350 dimensions. Similarity is measured by the angle between their vectors, using cosine similarity. This gives the system one common representation for comparing language items, with the structure learned from the passages in which words occur rather than from separately supplied judgments of their meanings.

The abstract reports good agreement with human judgments and behavior on multiple-choice vocabulary and domain-knowledge tests, expert essay evaluations, and other tasks. These findings show that the learned relationships can support more than a single text-comparison exercise. The paper also presents examples of applications for the knowledge extracted by this method.
neurips-1997-learning-human-like-knowled.tldr: SVD learns semantic spaces from word–passage relationships that reproduce aspects of human vocabulary knowledge and text judgments.

paragraphs: The paper proposes diffusion networks for modeling natural signals that vary continuously in time and space. These are recurrent neural networks with probabilistic dynamics, so their subject is the distribution of possible evolving paths. Learning therefore concerns how a signal changes over time, including the randomness in that evolution.

The main mathematical contribution is a formula for the gradient of a path's log likelihood with respect to the network's drift parameters. This gradient supplies a way to adjust the dynamics to make observed paths more likely. The approach works in the nonequilibrium regime and is proposed for problems related to system identification, state estimation, and signal filtering.

A further result concerns where and when learning information is needed. With a suitable activation function, including the stated quasi-linear sigmoidal example, the gradient is local in both space and time. The authors highlight this property for computational neuroscience and hardware design because it connects the learning formula to computations based on locally available information.
neurips-1997-learning-path-distributions.tldr: Diffusion networks learn continuous stochastic paths through a likelihood gradient that can be local in space and time.

paragraphs: A processor's execution speed can depend strongly on the order of the instructions it receives. Optimizing compilers therefore need scheduling heuristics that choose effective instruction orders. The paper addresses the cost of developing those heuristics by hand and asks whether supervised learning can produce them automatically.

The authors frame instruction scheduling as a learning task, concentrating on straight-line code, also called basic blocks. This scope provides a specific scheduling problem on which to learn and assess a heuristic. The approach uses features to represent the information available to the learned scheduler, making the choice of representation part of the practical solution.

Experiments on a real processor show that a small number of features can support quite good scheduling performance. Several supervised learning methods perform nearly optimally relative to those features. That qualification matters: the result concerns how well the methods use the chosen information. It suggests that automatically learned heuristics can make effective scheduling decisions from a compact representation.
neurips-1997-learning-to-schedule-straig.tldr: Supervised learning produces effective instruction-scheduling heuristics for basic blocks using only a few features.

paragraphs: MELONET I generates baroque-style music from a supplied melody. It creates a four-part chorale harmonization and a variation of any selected chorale voice. The system learns from pieces by composers including Bach and Pachelbel, with the aim of capturing musical organization beyond short sequences of neighboring notes.

Its architecture combines interacting feedforward networks that operate at different time scales with Kohonen networks that classify and recognize musical structure. The different time scales allow the system to address harmonic, motif, and phrase organization together. The abstract attributes its ability to learn these higher-order structures to this combination of interacting components.

The resulting works are chorale partitas in Pachelbel's style. Experts judged their quality comparable to improvisations by an experienced human organist. This is a reported judgment about the generated music, while the technical contribution is the organization of learning across musical time scales. The system connects local melodic variation with larger structures that help give a piece stylistic coherence.
neurips-1997-melonet-i-neural-nets-for-i.tldr: MELONET I combines neural networks across time scales to generate baroque chorale harmonizations and melodic variations.

paragraphs: Speech-recognition hidden Markov models use high-dimensional feature vectors to describe short stretches of sound. These features can become correlated when speech changes over time or when noise contaminates the signal. The paper investigates how to represent those relationships without requiring a large number of covariance parameters.

The proposed tool is factor analysis, which models covariance through a compact set of parameters. Those parameters are estimated using expectation-maximization, and the estimation procedure can be incorporated into hidden Markov model training. The authors also examine how factor analysis works alongside mixture densities, combining two ways of making the acoustic model more expressive.

The evaluation uses recognition of alphanumeric strings and keeps the total number of parameters fixed. Under that constraint, the authors find that properly combining mixture densities and factor analysis gives better models than either approach alone. The finding matters because the improvement comes from how modeling capacity is organized, rather than simply from allowing a larger parameter budget.
neurips-1997-modeling-acoustic-correlati.tldr: Combining factor analysis with mixture densities improves speech models at a fixed total parameter count.

paragraphs: The paper asks how difficult it is to train a neural network whose fit is close to the best possible fit within a chosen network class. The data consist of input vectors paired with real-valued outputs. Performance is assessed through the square root of the average squared prediction error.

The quantity studied is the gap between a candidate network's error and the smallest error achievable in its class. This distinction matters because the target is proximity to the best available network, even when that best network cannot fit the data perfectly. The paper examines whether training can reliably make this gap smaller than a fixed positive threshold.

For several classes of neural networks, achieving such a gap is proved NP-hard. The threshold does not depend on the number of data points, so the result concerns even a fixed level of approximation to the optimum. It establishes a computational obstacle to general guarantees of near-best training performance, with the claim applying to the network classes covered by the proofs.
neurips-1997-on-the-infeasibility-of-tra.tldr: For several neural-network classes, finding a fit within a fixed error gap of the optimum is NP-hard.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional perspective structure from two-dimensional point sets involves two connected questions: which points correspond, and what geometric transformation relates them. The paper proposes estimating these together. This matters because the geometry depends on the matches, while deciding which matches are plausible also depends on the geometry.

The method represents possible correspondences with a bipartite graph and places a mixture model over that representation. It then uses expectation-maximization to optimize the model. Correspondence is treated probabilistically, allowing the geometric estimation to account for uncertainty about which point pairings represent the same underlying structure.

Within this framework, the probabilities of structural correspondence control how much candidate matches contribute to the expected likelihood used to estimate perspective pose. Matches with little support can therefore have less influence on the geometric solution. The abstract identifies this as a mechanism for rejecting structural outliers. The contribution is a unified estimation procedure in which uncertain matching and pose recovery inform one another.
neurips-1997-recovering-perspective-pose.tldr: A joint EM model estimates perspective pose and point correspondences while reducing the influence of structural outliers.

paragraphs: The paper examines what computational mechanisms a recurrent neural network can develop through training. Earlier work had shown a network learning a simple context-free language by counting. Here, the authors extend that investigation to a harder language involving a simple palindrome, where the identity of symbols must also matter.

The trained network organizes its resources into a symbol-sensitive counting solution. This means its counting behavior carries information about symbols rather than merely recording a single undifferentiated total. The result connects language processing with an internal analog mechanism that emerges through learning, giving a concrete example alongside formal analyses of analog computation.

The authors also analyze the network as a dynamical system to explain how the solution operates. Their analysis shows that the network can count, copy counting information, and store it. The contribution therefore includes both successful learning of the language and an account of the internal operations that support it. These operations help explain how recurrent dynamics can coordinate information across a sequence.
neurips-1997-recurrent-neural-networks-c.tldr: A recurrent network learns a simple palindrome language by counting, copying, and storing symbol-dependent information.

paragraphs: The paper addresses regularization when training data arrive sequentially. In the setting described, cross-validation is unavailable for regularization or model selection, and bootstrapping is impractical for estimating confidence. This creates a need for training methods that manage estimation uncertainty within the sequential learning process itself.

The authors use a minimum-variance estimation approach based on the extended Kalman algorithm to train multilayer perceptrons. Their main theoretical contribution is to connect this approach with variable learning-rate algorithms and a Bayesian estimation framework. These links bring together methods that describe adaptation from different perspectives: estimation uncertainty, changing update rates, and probabilistic learning.

Using these connections, the paper proposes algorithms intended to remove heuristic choices of initial conditions and noise covariance matrices in Kalman-based training. Those choices determine how the estimation process starts and represents uncertainty. The contribution is therefore both an explanation of relationships among learning frameworks and a route toward more principled configuration of sequential neural-network training.
neurips-1997-regularisation-in-sequentia.tldr: Links between Kalman filtering, adaptive learning rates, and Bayesian estimation support more principled regularization in sequential learning.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a memory problem in learning probabilistic transducers represented by suffix trees. These models use contexts to describe conditional output distributions, but the existing learning approach can build very large trees. Storing the resulting representation can therefore require a great deal of computer memory.

The proposed model makes the representation more compact by sharing distribution parameters across contexts that produce similar conditional outputs. Different contexts can retain their role in describing the input while relying on common parameters when their output behavior is alike. The central idea is to organize storage around similarities in predictive behavior, reducing the need for separate parameter sets.

The authors illustrate the approach through comparative experiments on learning a noun phrase recognizer. This application tests the compact transducer in a language-processing setting where context helps determine output. The stated contribution is a more economical model and learning algorithm, with the experiments demonstrating advantages of sharing parameters among contexts instead of allowing the tree representation to grow so large.
neurips-1997-shared-context-probabilisti.tldr: Sharing parameters among contexts with similar output distributions makes learned probabilistic transducers more compact.

paragraphs: The paper develops an image-retrieval algorithm intended to approximate how visually similar images appear. Its central problem is choosing a representation in which meaningful visual resemblance becomes measurable. The method converts images into a feature space that captures structure, texture, and color through a tree of filters.

Similarity is then defined through distance in that feature space: closer representations correspond to greater similarity. This gives an example-based search system a concrete way to compare a supplied image with stored images. The authors use the algorithm to construct a retrieval system for large image databases, connecting the perceptual representation directly to a search application.

Evaluation uses carefully designed target sets in which variation is restricted to one visual characteristic at a time. This makes the comparisons more focused by separating different aspects of visual appearance. The authors quantitatively compare retrieval rates with standard methods. The contribution combines a structure-aware image representation, an operational database system, and a controlled approach to assessing visual retrieval behavior.
neurips-1997-structure-driven-image-data.tldr: A filter-tree representation supports example-based image search using distances that reflect structure, texture, and color.

paragraphs: The paper studies how quickly Q-learning approaches its limiting solution after many updates. Its analysis concerns discounted Markov decision processes with a discount factor greater than one half. The central question is how the eventual learning rate depends on both discounting and the frequency with which different state-action pairs are encountered.

For sampling from a fixed probability distribution, the result uses the ratio between the smallest and largest state-action occupation frequencies. This ratio describes how unevenly the learning process visits different pairs. The stated rate has two regimes, separated according to whether the product of this ratio and one minus the discount factor falls below one half.

The authors extend the results to convergent online learning using occupation frequencies from the stationary distribution. That extension requires the minimum occupation frequency to be positive, so every state-action pair covered by the result must continue receiving visits. The analysis ties asymptotic learning speed to sampling balance and discounting, making those conditions explicit parts of the convergence account.
neurips-1997-the-asymptotic-convergence-.tldr: Q-learning's asymptotic convergence rate depends on discounting and how evenly state-action pairs are sampled.

paragraphs: A one-nearest-neighbor classifier bases its decision on the closest stored example, making the definition of distance central to its behavior. The paper studies the Canonical Distortion Measure as a principled choice of distance and proves its optimality for one-nearest-neighbor classification within the framework considered.

The authors also establish a connection to familiar feature-based distances. When the relevant function class consists of linear combinations of a fixed collection of features, the Canonical Distortion Measure becomes squared Euclidean distance in that feature space. This links the abstract measure to a concrete procedure: represent examples through the chosen features and compare their squared distances.

The paper provides PAC-like bounds on the number of samples required to learn the measure. It also presents an experiment in which a neural network learns a Canonical Distortion Measure for Japanese optical character recognition and then supplies the distance for nearest-neighbor classification. Together, the theory and application treat similarity as something grounded in the learning problem and potentially learned from examples.
neurips-1997-the-canonical-distortion-me.tldr: The Canonical Distortion Measure provides a theoretically grounded distance for nearest-neighbor classification and reduces to feature-space squared distance in a stated setting.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether computations associated with complex visual cells can occur within a single neuron's dendrites. It builds on evidence challenging a purely hierarchical account in which complex cells depend on pooled simple-cell input. The alternative uses nonlinear interactions among synaptic inputs within an excitable dendritic tree.

The authors extend an earlier biophysical modeling result to binocular disparity tuning, which concerns differences between the images presented to the two eyes. In an isolated model pyramidal cell, they demonstrate tuning at a spatial resolution much finer than the overall receptive field. This shows how fine selectivity can emerge within the modeled cell's broader input region.

The model also exhibits systematic shifts in preferred disparity for rivalrous light and dark bar pairs. Both findings agree with experimental reports described in the abstract. The results support the potential role of computations inside dendrites in binocular processing. Because the demonstration uses an isolated model cell, its contribution is a concrete account of how those responses could arise through intradendritic interactions.
neurips-1997-toward-a-single-cell-accoun.tldr: A biophysical neuron model reproduces binocular disparity responses through nonlinear computations within its dendrites.

paragraphs: The paper addresses hierarchical clustering when data arrive over time and their characteristics change. In this setting, the organization discovered from earlier observations may need to adapt as new observations appear. The authors propose an unsupervised online algorithm that estimates a hierarchy through a decision tree.

The tree is derived using the principle of minimum cross entropy. Alongside that statistical criterion, the algorithm uses a metalearning idea, described as learning to learn, to adapt to changes in the data. The approach therefore combines a method for constructing groups with a mechanism for adjusting learning as the source changes, making adaptation central to the clustering procedure.

The authors demonstrate efficiency on two applications: grouping artificial data from a non-stationary source and hierarchical segmentation of LANDSAT images. These examples connect the method to both changing data distributions and image organization. The contribution is an adaptive way to build hierarchical structure online, allowing the grouping process to respond to the characteristics of the data it receives.
neurips-1997-unsupervised-on-line-learni.tldr: An online clustering algorithm combines minimum cross entropy and metalearning to adapt hierarchical decision trees to changing data.
